section: Analytics Job Market and Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Analytics Job Market and Skill Gap Analysis
Boston University, AD 688 | Academic team project | Python, PySpark, scikit-learn, Quarto
Objective. Evaluate career opportunities for analytics professionals in the computer systems design industry and identify the skills that candidates should prioritize.
Approach. From a source dataset of more than 500,000 job postings, the team constructed an analytical panel of 1,790 recent analytics roles. We measured employer demand by skill, benchmarked that demand against the team’s own proficiency to produce a prioritized development plan, and built classification models to identify the factors associated with higher-paying roles. When the initial industry selection produced too few postings for reliable analysis, we revised the scope and documented the change.



Most requested skills in analytics job postings.


Outcome.

Python and SQL each appear in more than 60% of postings, well ahead of all other skills.
The median advertised salary was $151,475, and 41% of postings offered remote or hybrid work.
Job title alone identified higher-paying postings with 59% accuracy. A model incorporating skills, location, and education reached 78%.
The skills most strongly associated with higher pay were not those most frequently requested.

View the project on GitHub

section: New York City Real Estate Market Analysis
text:
New York City Real Estate Market Analysis
Boston University | Academic team project | Python, Power BI
Objective. Identify and explain residential market trends across New York City neighborhoods.
Approach. The team prepared and analyzed the data in Python and presented the results through interactive Power BI dashboards.
Outcome.

A group of neighborhoods experienced sharp increases in residential prices.
A second group tracked closely with industrial investment in the surrounding area.
A third group continued to decline in value while population growth exceeded the capacity of the local housing stock.

title: Projects
text:
In-House Brewery Business Case
Boston University | Academic team project | Business case development
Objective. Assess whether a pub should bring brewing in house to produce its own line of IPAs.
Approach. Over one semester, the team developed an end-to-end business case covering market positioning, marketing strategy, and the operational requirements of in-house production.
Outcome. The analysis supported the investment. Initial losses narrowed over the first several years, and in-house production strengthened the pub’s community presence and supported longer-term market development.
Competencies: business case development, operations planning, marketing strategy

title: Jenna DeRosa
text: Supply chains run on two things: relationships and data. I have spent five years building the first, and I am finishing a master’s degree to master the second.

title: Jenna DeRosa
text:
What I Do
I lead global distribution sourcing at Prodrive Technologies, shaping how a high-tech manufacturer works with its distribution partners around the world. I set sourcing strategy, manage the supplier relationships behind it, and design the processes that make strategic sourcing repeatable.
Semiconductors are among the most complex products in the world to make and to move. A single component can pass through several countries before it reaches a production line, lead times are long, and capacity cannot be added quickly. Two forces have reshaped my role in recent years. The first is artificial intelligence: demand for AI hardware has redrawn the market, shifting where capacity goes and changing availability and pricing for everyone else. The second is geopolitics: trade policy, export controls, and tariffs now influence sourcing decisions as much as price and lead time do. Sourcing in this environment means planning for a market that does not stand still.

title: Jenna DeRosa
text:
Where Supply Chain Meets Data
The best supply chain decisions I have seen were made by people who understood both the business and the systems that record it. The weakest were driven by metrics that looked precise and measured the wrong thing.
That is what led me to a Master of Science in Supply Chain Management with a concentration in Data Analytics at Boston University, which I complete in December 2026. My goal was never to become an engineer. It was to become fluent enough to stand between the people who build data tools and the people who depend on them: to follow how information moves through SAP and out to suppliers, and to design KPIs that reflect how an operation really runs.

title: Jenna DeRosa
text:
From Fashion to Semiconductors
My background is less conventional than my job title suggests. I studied Fashion Business Management at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York, an industry where supply chains are global, fast, and unforgiving. I started in purchasing at W.B. Mason, entered the semiconductor market as a buyer at Fusion Worldwide, and then joined Prodrive Technologies, in a role that took me from the United States to the Netherlands.

title: Jenna DeRosa
text:
What I Am Working Toward
Strategic supply chain development and process design are the work I enjoy most. I am building toward leading the teams that do it.

title: Jenna DeRosa
text:
Outside of Work
I am fascinated by the history of global trade and how centuries of routes, ports, and agreements shaped the supply chains we manage today. It is a useful perspective to have when trade policy is rewriting them again. I share my home with Paxton, a miniature Australian shepherd who has no interest in any of it.
